subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and empagliflozin is admitted with 2 days of nausea, vomiting, and malaise after a viral illness with reduced oral intake. Glucose is 186 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.19, bicarbonate 9 mEq/L, anion gap 26 mEq/L, and beta-hydroxybutyrate 7.2 mmol/L; urine ketones are positive.
question: Which of the following best explains the development of ketoacidosis with only modest hyperglycemia in this patient?

options.text: Reduced glomerular filtration of ketone bodies
Increased hepatic ketogenesis driven by a low insulin-to-glucagon ratio
Impaired ketone body oxidation in skeletal muscle
Osmotic diuresis causing a contraction alkalosis

explanation_correct: Because empagliflozin causes glucosuria, plasma glucose can remain only mildly elevated even as ketoacidosis develops. Reduced carbohydrate availability plus the stress of illness lowers the insulin-to-glucagon ratio, which stimulates adipose lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, so beta-hydroxybutyrate rises and produces an anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Impaired renal ketone clearance is not the primary event; the acidosis is driven by overproduction of ketoacids rather than by reduced filtration.
explanation_incorrect.C: Skeletal muscle retains the ability to oxidize ketone bodies; a defect in their use would not raise their plasma concentration.
explanation_incorrect.D: Metformin can cause lactic acidosis, but the elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate and positive ketones here identify ketoacidosis as the cause of the anion gap.
explanation_incorrect.E: Osmotic diuresis may accompany glucosuria, but a contraction alkalosis would lower, not raise, the anion gap and does not explain the ketones.

educationalObjective: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycemic ketoacidosis because glucosuria masks hyperglycemia while a low insulin-to-glucagon ratio drives hepatic ketogenesis.
